name: Biomolecules (Chemistry)
description: Corrected Chemistry Biomolecules flashcards covering carbohydrates, proteins, enzymes, vitamins, and hormones.

cards.definition: All monosaccharides and the disaccharides maltose and lactose are reducing sugars.
Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because its reducing groups are involved in the glycosidic bond.
A glycosidic bond links two monosaccharide units.
Sucrose is formed from α-D-glucose and β-D-fructose through an α,β-1,2-glycosidic linkage between C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose.
Maltose is formed from two α-D-glucose units through an α-1,4-glycosidic linkage between C1 and C4.
Lactose is formed from β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose through a β-1,4-glycosidic linkage between C1 of galactose and C4 of glucose.
Starch is the major storage polysaccharide in plants. It is a polymer of α-D-glucose and has two components: amylose and amylopectin.
Amylose is the water-soluble, unbranched component of starch, about 15–20%. It contains about 200–1000 α-D-glucose units joined mainly by α-1,4-glycosidic linkages.
Amylopectin is the water-insoluble, branched component of starch, about 80–85%. It has α-1,4 linkages in chains and α-1,6 linkages at branch points.
Cellulose is the most abundant organic substance in the plant kingdom. It is a straight-chain polysaccharide of β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4-glycosidic linkages.

Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals, also called animal starch. It is structurally similar to amylopectin but more highly branched, and is stored mainly in liver and muscles. It is also found in yeast and fungi.
The two aldopentoses found in nucleic acids are D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose.

cards.term: Water solubility of glucose and sucrose
cards.definition: Glucose and sucrose are water-soluble because they form hydrogen bonds with water. Benzene is non-polar and cannot form such hydrogen bonds.

cards.term: Absence of free aldehyde group in glucose pentaacetate
cards.definition: Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine to form an oxime, showing that it has no free aldehydic (-CHO) group.
Proteins are among the most abundant biomolecules in living systems. The word protein comes from Greek proteios, meaning primary or of prime importance.

Amino acids are colourless, crystalline, water-soluble, high-melting solids. They behave like salts because they contain both amino (-NH2) and carboxyl (-COOH) groups. α-amino acids are the biologically important amino acids found in proteins.
Amino acids are represented by three-letter symbols and sometimes one-letter symbols, for example glycine = Gly or G.

Essential amino acids must be obtained from the diet. Common human essential amino acids are valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and histidine. Arginine is conditionally essential, especially during growth.
The main aromatic amino acids are phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan. Histidine has an aromatic imidazole ring but is usually grouped as a basic amino acid in simple classification.
Methionine and cysteine contain sulphur.
Aspartic acid and glutamic acid are acidic amino acids and are negatively charged at body pH.
Lysine, arginine, and histidine are basic amino acids.
A zwitterion is a dipolar ion with both positive and negative charges but overall neutral charge. Amino acids show zwitterionic form and are amphoteric.
All standard amino acids except glycine are optically active and can exist as D and L forms.
In L-amino acids, the -NH2 group is on the left side in Fischer projection.
Most naturally occurring amino acids in proteins occur in the L-configuration.
A peptide bond is an amide bond formed between the -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH2 group of another, with elimination of water. A dipeptide contains two amino acids.
When the -COOH group of glycine combines with the -NH2 group of alanine, the dipeptide formed is glycylalanine.

Chains with more than about 10 amino acids are called polypeptides. When the number of amino acids exceeds about 100 and molecular mass is above about 10,000 u, it is generally called a protein, but the boundary is not sharp.
Insulin has 51 amino acids and is still considered a protein because it has a well-defined conformation and biological activity.
Primary structure is the specific sequence of amino acids in one or more polypeptide chains. Different sequences produce different proteins.
Secondary structure increaseludes α-helix and β-pleated sheet, stabilized mainly by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the peptide backbone.

Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of a protein. Fibrous proteins are elongated and usually water-insoluble, while globular proteins are folded into compact spherical shapes and are often soluble.
Fibrous proteins have parallel polypeptide chains held by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bonds. Examples increaselude keratin and myosin.
Globular proteins are folded into compact spherical shapes and are generally soluble. Examples increaselude insulin and albumin.
Quaternary structure is the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits in a protein.
A protein found in a biological system with its unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein.
Denaturation destroys the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein while usually leaving the primary structure intact. The protein loses its biological activity.
Almost all enzymes are globular proteins. Maltase converts maltose into glucose. Sucrase lowers the activation energy for sucrose hydrolysis compared with acid hydrolysis.

Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal growth, health, and specific biological functions. Excess intake of some vitamins can be harmful. The word came from vital amine, but the final e was dropped when it was found that many vitamins are not amines.
Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble and water-insoluble. They are stored in liver and adipose tissue.
Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins are water-soluble and generally need regular supply because they are excreted in urine. Vitamin B12 is an exception because it can be stored.
Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia, hardening/drying of the cornea, and night blindness.
Vitamin B1 is thiamine. Its deficiency causes beriberi, loss of appetite, and stunted growth.
Vitamin B2 is riboflavin. Its deficiency can cause cheilosis, digestive disorders, and burning sensation of the skin.
Vitamin B6 is pyridoxine. Its deficiency can cause convulsions.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anaemia, with reduced RBC formation and haemoglobin-related problems.
Vitamin C is ascorbic acid. Its deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia, soft bones and joint pain, in adults.
Vitamin E deficiency can cause increasereased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness. Sources increaselude vegetable oils such as wheat germ oil and sunflower oil.
Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting. Deficiency increasereases blood-clotting time and can cause bleeding. It is found in green leafy vegetables.
Har Gobind Khorana helped decreaseipher the genetic code.

Hormones are intercellular chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands and released directly into blood. Steroids increaselude androgens and estrogens, polypeptide hormones increaselude insulin and endorphins, and amino-acid derivatives increaselude epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Insulin helps keep blood glucose within a narrow range. It is released when blood glucose level rises.
Glucagon increasereases blood glucose level. Together, insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose homeostasis.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli, especially stress responses.

Thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland and is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid tyrosine. Low thyroxine causes hypothyroidism, lethargy, obesity, and enlarged thyroid gland. High thyroxine causes hyperthyroidism.

Steroid hormones are produced by the adrenal cortex and gonads. Glucocorticoids regulate carbohydrate metabolism, modulate inflammation, and participate in stress response. Mineralocorticoids regulate salt and water balance through the kidney.

Improper function or under-secretion of adrenal cortex hormones can cause Addison's disease, with hypoglycaemia, weakness, and increasereased susceptibility to stress. It can be fatal unless treated with mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids.
Estradiol is the primary female sex hormone. It helps develop secondary female sexual characters and regulates the menstrual cycle.
Progesterone prepares the uterus for implantation and supports pregnancy.
